prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength allow clock accuracy at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I move my preferred configuration from spherical-aberration correction (B008) to optical lattice clocks (B025). The reason is the test I apply to every candidate: the original experiment, verified independently, with the people who did it identifiable. The magic-wavelength lattice is one idea with one clear origin, Katori's proposal and his group's first demonstration with strontium, in which Takamoto was a member of the group and so is part of the same credit and not a rival claim. The 10^-18 performance was then reached and cross-checked in more than one institution, so we do not rely on a single laboratory's word. It also opens a door in the sense I care about: relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-matter searches are now measurements people can make. Four colleagues who differ in field prefer it and name identical laureates, and all the others who discuss it call it mature and cleanly attributed. For a committee that has to be absolutely sure about topic and names, that is the strongest position on the shortlist. I would ask that the citation be confined to the lattice clock and say nothing of the Th-229 nuclear clock or of the comb.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is precision metrology and that Ye's clocks stand on the frequency comb prized in 2005, next to the ion-control prize of 2012. I do not dismiss it. My answer is that the new element is the lattice trapping with the light shift cancelled, which none of the earlier prizes covers, and that capability prizes for tools that changed what can be observed are in the tradition of the Physics Prize, as the electron microscope itself was in 1986. That answer holds only if the citation is tight. A second weakness is the early contributions of Lemonde and the SYRTE group, of PTB and NIST, and of the theory of the magic wavelength. I have not seen the expert record on this and say so. Finally, I give up B008, which I believe is a genuine invention, because the TEM and STEM corrector claims are unresolved and because I am a biased judge of my own field.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B025 as a new measurement capability that is reproduced across independent laboratories, treats Takamoto's Sr demonstration as part of Katori's own group, and says the citation must be drawn tightly to keep out the Th-229 nuclear clock and the many-body clock work. He also discloses a mentor-lineage link through John Hall.
responses.response: Stefan's treatment of Takamoto as part of Katori's group is the answer I asked for in round 1, and it removes my main priority concern, since the first lattice-clock demonstration then sits with Katori and the two names stand. I still want the experts to confirm the dates. On his disclosure, a year in Hall's laboratory during a PhD is a lineage link and not a collaboration with Katori or Ye. I would regard it as disclosure and not recusal, and I would accept the Chair's judgement. I would also support his tight wording: lattice clock only.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what exactly the new discovery in B025 is, as opposed to a long sequence of accuracy improvements built on the comb, and says that if it is the magic-wavelength lattice and many-body clock the citation can say so and he finds it timely. He prefers B036.
responses.response: Bernhard is right that accuracy alone is not a discovery. My answer is that the discovery is the magic-wavelength lattice, a way of holding many atoms with the light shift cancelled on the clock transition, which removes Doppler and recoil effects and allows the statistics that reach 10^-18. That is a new principle and not a refinement of the comb. I would put it in the citation, and I do not propose crediting the later accuracy records for themselves. On B036 I find his Z2 argument against the 2016 overlap persuasive. My difficulty is the missing Bernevig and Hughes, which he names himself, and that is why B036 is my second alternative and not my choice.

responses.point: Eriksson states that B008 is a genuine invention with a clear Rose, Haider and Urban chain but would hesitate to reward an enabling instrument, and says the Krivanek claim for STEM correctors is a real complication. He prefers B036 and lists B025 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Olle's two reservations about B008 are ones I share. Aberration correction is an enabling tool and the TEM and STEM claims are not settled, so it would be wrong of me to hold a configuration on which I am conflicted and which only two of us ranked. I do not agree that a tool is of lower rank by that fact, and I make the same argument for clocks. I am glad that he can accept B025 and would be content. Compared with B036 I weigh the credit gap more heavily: a trio that leaves out Bernevig and Hughes is a larger risk than the lattice-clock questions about early contributors.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B025 and says the original demonstration, not the most precise one, should decide credit, and she asks whether the early work of Lemonde, Takamoto and others is fully settled in the record. She also warns of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with Eva that the original demonstration is the test. I would still ask her, as the atomic structure expert here, to confirm that the light-shift and blackbody evaluation behind the 10^-18 claim is robust and not model-dependent, because the chair put that question to her and my confidence relies on her answer. If the evaluation holds, then the 2005 and 2012 overlap is a question of wording and not of substance. Her comment on Ye's Th-229 work convinces me to exclude it explicitly.

uncertainties: Whether the experts confirm that Katori's group, including Takamoto, made the first demonstration of a lattice clock, and what the contributions of Lemonde, SYRTE, PTB and NIST add to the credit.
Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a discovery distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a robust, reproduced evaluation of systematic shifts at 10^-18 supports the claim, which I cannot judge as an atomic physicist.
Whether a later committee should return to aberration correction, and how the TEM and STEM claims of Rose, Haider and Urban against Krivanek, Dellby and Batson would then be divided.
Whether Cao and other experimentalists would have to be added to B022 if the committee moves there.
statement.conflict_note: I withdraw B008 as my preference, in part because I am an electron microscopist and the current President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, and I would not wish to drive a decision in my own field. My profile documents no tie to Rose, Urban, Haider or Krivanek, and I would accept a recusal discussion on B008 if it came back. I know of no connection to Katori or Ye, to Hall, or to any other credited person on B025, B022 or B036. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which does not touch any candidate on the shortlist. I note Kroll's disclosure about Hall and regard it as disclosure rather than a reason for recusal.
